common_name: Golden Girl Panda Plant (Golden-Leaved Kalanchoe Tomentosa)

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in dry, gritty succulent mix and keep in bright light; the warm gold leaf color develops fully only under strong sun, fading toward grey-green in shade.

directions: 'Golden Girl' is a panda plant selection that trades the species' cool blue-grey tone for warm yellow-gold, felted leaves while keeping the characteristic reddish-brown scalloped margins. Bright, direct light is essential to bring out the gold color and keep growth compact; plants kept too dim stretch and revert to duller green-grey tones. Water at the soil line and allow the mix to dry completely between waterings, since the dense leaf fuzz traps moisture and invites rot if splashed overhead. Pinch or cut back leggy stems to keep the naturally single-stemmed habit full and shrubby.

planting.note: Take stem cuttings and let the cut end callus for a day or two before setting in dry, fast-draining succulent mix; this selection stays far more compact than the straight species.

directions: 'Roseleaf' is a long-cultivated dwarf selection long sold as a Kalanchoe beharensis cultivar, bearing upright, stocky stems of triangular, velvety, silvery-green leaves with softly serrated, wavy edges. It stays far more compact than the towering species, typically holding under a foot tall and wide in cultivation, which suits it to windowsills and small containers where full-size felt bush would quickly outgrow the space. Give it the brightest light available, since low light causes weak, stretched growth, and let the soil dry out fully between waterings to avoid stem and root rot. Its dense, upright form needs little pruning beyond removing the occasional leggy stem.

planting.note: Propagate from offsets or leaf cuttings in gritty succulent mix; variegation is unstable and stems that revert to solid green should be removed to keep the plant colorful.

directions: 'Fantastic' is a patented variegated sport of flapjack plant, its thick, stacked, paddle-shaped leaves streaked in cream, yellow, and green and often blushed red along the margins in strong light. Because the pale variegated tissue lacks the chlorophyll that shields the leaves from sun, give it bright light with some protection from harsh summer afternoon sun to prevent scorch, rather than the full, unshaded exposure the plain green species tolerates. Water deeply and then let the rosette dry out completely, watering roughly every 2-4 weeks depending on season, and keep water off the leaf surface to avoid spotting. Watch for all-green reversion shoots and cut them out at the base so they don't outcompete the variegated growth.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; this old English selection sets little to no fruit, so it avoids the litter of spiny seed balls common to seedling sweetgum.

directions: Worplesdon is a long-cultivated English selection prized for its finely dissected, star-shaped leaves that emerge light green, deepen to glossy dark green through summer, and finish in a reliable blend of red, orange, and yellow each autumn. It sets seed sparingly compared with the species, so it produces far fewer of the prickly gumballs that make standard sweetgum unwelcome near patios and walkways. Grow it in full sun in moist, well-drained soil, transplanting young container stock since sweetgums develop a taproot that resents disturbance once established. Its dense, rounded-pyramidal crown makes it a dependable shade tree for parks, campuses, and larger home landscapes.

planting.note: Plant in spring in full sun and moist, well-drained soil; Palo Alto was selected specifically for producing vivid fall color even in mild-winter regions where seedling sweetgums often color poorly.

directions: Selected in California for consistent autumn performance in climates too mild to reliably color most sweetgums, Palo Alto reddens early and dependably, moving through dark glossy red, orange, and a final rich burgundy before leaf drop. It grows in a narrower, more upright pyramidal form than seedling sweetgum, making it a good fit for tighter side yards and street tree strips. Plant in full sun in moist, well-drained soil, and expect it to produce the species' textured bark and spiny seed balls, so keep it away from walkways and turf where litter is a concern. It is otherwise nearly trouble-free, tolerating a range of soils once established.

planting.note: Plant in full sun in moist, well-drained soil; Burgundy is valued for holding its wine-red fall foliage weeks longer than typical sweetgum, often into early winter.

directions: Burgundy stands out among sweetgum selections for how long it clings to its foliage, carrying a deep wine-purple color well past the point when other sweetgums have already dropped their leaves. Young trees grow conical, filling out into an evenly branched pyramidal shade tree with attractively corky, furrowed bark on older wood. It adapts to a wide range of soil types and tolerates both moist and average garden conditions once its roots are established, though it colors most intensely in full sun. Because it still bears the species' spiny seed balls, site it away from lawns, patios, and pathways.

planting.note: Plant in full sun in moist, well-drained, preferably acidic soil; Festival's narrow, upright habit and softer pastel fall coloring set it apart from broader-spreading sweetgum selections.

directions: Festival is grown for its tall, slender, narrow-pyramidal profile, considerably tighter than seedling sweetgum, which suits it to street plantings and smaller properties where a broad canopy would not fit. Its fall display leans toward softer pastel tones of peach, pink, and gold rather than the deep reds typical of the species, giving it a distinct look in the autumn landscape. It performs best in full sun on moist, well-drained, acidic to neutral soil, where its color develops most vividly. Like other sweetgums it produces spiky seed balls and a taproot when young, so transplant container-grown stock while small.

planting.note: Plant grafted stock in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Gum Ball is a true dwarf, staying compact enough for patios and courtyards.

directions: Discovered as a naturally occurring dwarf branch mutation, Gumball is typically grafted onto a standard trunk to form a dense, rounded, multi-stemmed mophead only a few feet tall and wide at maturity, a fraction the size of seedling sweetgum. Its deeply lobed leaves emerge light green, darken to glossy green through summer, and finish in bright orange, red, and purple tones each fall. The compact rounded crown and deeply ridged gray bark also give it interest through the bare winter months, and it sets little to none of the spiny seed balls that make full-size sweetgum a nuisance underfoot. Grow it in full sun to light shade in moist, well-drained soil for use as a specimen shrub or small accent tree in tight spaces.

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Sheri's Cloud must be propagated by grafting onto seedling rootstock since it will not come true from seed.

directions: Discovered as a chance roadside mutation in Arkansas, Sheri's Cloud is the first widely available variegated black gum, its gray-green leaves edged in a bold creamy-white margin that brightens the canopy from spring through summer. In fall the variegated foliage shifts into soft tones of pink and red rather than the solid scarlet of straight-species black gum, giving it a softer, two-toned autumn display. Because the mutation is unstable from seed, plants are propagated by grafting onto Nyssa sylvatica rootstock, so young trees should be planted in spring and given a season to establish their deep taproot. Grow it as the species is grown, in full sun on moist, acidic, well-drained soil, avoiding high-pH or urban-polluted sites.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; fall planting lets roots establish before Weroma's autumn-into-winter bloom season.

directions: Weroma is a compact, low-spreading Australian-raised sasanqua cultivar producing an abundance of small, single to semi-double white flowers with a boss of golden stamens from fall into early winter. Its dense, wide-spreading, naturally mounding habit stays well under other sasanquas' size, making it a popular choice for a low evergreen groundcover, foundation planting, or the front of a mixed shrub border where a spilling, informal white drift is wanted. Grow in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil with some afternoon shade in hotter climates, since sasanquas bloom heaviest with several hours of direct sun but appreciate protection during the most intense summer heat. Feed with an acid-forming camellia fertilizer in early spring and again right after bloom, and shear or prune lightly only immediately after flowering to preserve next year's buds.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; fall planting establishes roots ahead of Paradise Hilda's fall bloom season.

directions: Paradise Hilda is one of Australian breeder Bob Cherry's compact 'Paradise' series sasanquas, valued for its small, double, soft pink flowers set against fine-textured, glossy dark-green foliage on a naturally low, dense, spreading frame. The tidy, slow-growing habit fits foundation plantings, low hedging, and mixed borders where a full-size sasanqua would quickly outgrow the space, while still delivering a heavy fall-into-winter bloom display typical of the group. Grow in acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to filtered sun, giving afternoon protection in the hottest climates. Feed with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and after bloom, and prune only immediately after flowering since buds set on the current season's wood for the following fall.

planting.note: Sow indoors 10-12 weeks before the last frost and transplant once seedlings are pencil-thick; direct seeding is possible in early spring but adds 20-30 days to maturity.

directions: Biker is an F1 hybrid leek with upright, tidy foliage and shanks that bulk up quickly through the mid-early season, resisting bulbing and staying easy to clean at harvest. Set pencil-thick transplants 4-6 inches apart in fertile soil with a pH of 6.2-6.8, and hill or trench soil around the stems two or three times as they grow to lengthen the blanched white shank. It holds good eating quality even at a large size and shows intermediate resistance to common rust, purple blotch, and white tip. Harvest through summer and fall and store several weeks near freezing in a humid cooler.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, or sow several seeds per pot and separate seedlings for transplanting into a shallow trench.

directions: Chinook is a fast-growing, adaptable F1 leek bred for reliable summer production, reaching harvest size faster than most fall and winter types. Grow in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil at pH 6.0-7.0, spacing plants 4-5 inches apart in rows 12-18 inches apart. Despite its quick summer maturity it is frost-hardy, and in mild climates can be left in the ground and harvested through winter or stored in the ground until the soil freezes.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, planting into a 5-inch-deep trench and filling in gradually as plants grow to blanch the shanks.

directions: Comanche is a high-yielding, adaptable F1 leek especially favored in Pacific Northwest gardens for its clean, upright habit and long, thick white shanks under dark blue-green flags. It performs well as both a summer and fall crop, and gradually filling the planting trench with soil as the plants grow lengthens the blanched shank for a milder, more tender base. Harvest young at finger size for a mild flavor or let stems reach a half-inch or more in diameter for fuller texture. It tolerates frost well and holds in the garden into the fall harvest window.

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant seedlings into holes about 6 inches deep, spaced roughly 6 inches apart; can also be sown thinly outdoors in early spring and transplanted later.

directions: Hannibal is a reliable, heavy-cropping leek that matures early and heavily, producing long, thick white shafts under dark green leaves from midsummer well into fall. It can be grown at closer spacing and pulled young as an excellent baby leek, or left to size up for a standard harvest. With soil mounded around the base and a layer of mulch, Hannibal tolerates cold well and can overwinter in the ground for a late harvest in mild climates.

planting.note: Start seed indoors in late winter, about 8-10 weeks before the last frost, and transplant into the garden in spring for an early-maturing crop.

directions: Zermatt, also sold as Swiss Giant Zermatt, is an early European leek that reaches harvest size faster than most fall or winter types, making it a good lead-in variety ahead of longer-season leeks like Tadorna in a succession planting. It grows tall with a sweeter, more delicate flavor than onion, well suited to creamy soups and light braises. Grow in well-drained soil with consistent moisture and harvest before hard freezes arrive, since it lacks the deep winter hardiness of true storage leeks.

common_name: Nanho Alba Butterfly Bush (Compact White Buddleja)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Nanho Alba is the white-flowered counterpart to Nanho Blue and Nanho Purple, sharing the same compact, fine-textured habit.

directions: Nanho Alba, also sold as Nanho White, completes the Nanho series alongside Nanho Blue and Nanho Purple, sharing its narrow, silver-gray, finely textured foliage and compact 4-6 foot habit on an arching, vase-shaped frame. Its long, tapering spikes of pure white, honey-scented flowers open from summer through fall and are heavily visited by butterflies, skippers, and hummingbirds, earning the cultivar an RHS Award of Garden Merit. Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun, since overly rich or wet conditions produce lax, floppy growth. In colder zones the top growth dies back over winter; cut the whole plant to 12-18 inches in late winter to keep the compact habit and maximize summer bloom.

common_name: Lo & Behold Blue Chip Jr. Butterfly Bush (Extra-Dwarf Early-Blooming Sterile Buddleja)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Blue Chip Jr. stays smaller than the original Blue Chip, fitting tight borders and large containers.

directions: Blue Chip Jr. is a further-refined selection within the Lo & Behold series, smaller and earlier to flower than the original Blue Chip, opening its lavender-blue spikes as much as two weeks ahead of other series members and continuing in a tight, mounded flush from early summer to frost. Like its siblings it is bred sterile, so energy that would otherwise go into seed production instead fuels continuous reblooming without deadheading. Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun, and cut the entire plant back hard in late winter to renew flowering wood and preserve its tailored, compact shape. Its diminutive scale makes it well suited to small borders, foundation plantings, and mixed containers where even Blue Chip would eventually crowd its neighbors.

common_name: Lo & Behold Lilac Chip Butterfly Bush (Dwarf Sterile Lavender-Pink Buddleja)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Lilac Chip's rounded, compact habit needs little upkeep beyond an annual hard cutback.

directions: Lilac Chip carries soft lavender-pink flower spikes on a dense, evenly rounded dwarf frame, part of the sterile Lo & Behold series bred to bloom continuously from summer straight through frost without deadheading. Its compact, well-behaved habit and deer-resistant foliage suit small borders, foundation plantings, and mixed containers where larger butterfly bush cultivars would need constant restraint. Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun, since overly rich soil encourages soft, floppy growth at the expense of flower density. Cut the entire plant back hard in late winter to renew flowering wood and keep its tidy, mounded shape.

common_name: Lo & Behold Pink Micro Chip Butterfly Bush (Ultra-Dwarf Sterile Pink Buddleja)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Pink Micro Chip is the smallest-growing member of the Lo & Behold series, ideal for tight spots and patio pots.

directions: Pink Micro Chip is the most diminutive selection in the sterile Lo & Behold series, forming a tight, mounded cushion of orchid-pink flower spikes that appear in flushes from early through late summer on new wood. Because it sets little to no viable seed, the plant channels its energy into repeated bloom cycles rather than seed production, and needs no deadheading to keep flowering into fall. Site it in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun with at least six hours of direct light for the densest flowering. Cut the entire plant back hard in late winter to renew wood and maintain its compact, rounded profile, which suits rock gardens, small borders, and container plantings where even other dwarf butterfly bush selections would grow too large.

common_name: Buzz Sky Blue Butterfly Bush (Dwarf Compact Pale Blue Buddleja)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Buzz Sky Blue keeps the fountain-shaped form of the Buzz series on a footprint small enough for large containers.

directions: Buzz Sky Blue produces dense, pale sky-blue flower panicles with a contrasting orange eye on a shrub condensed to roughly a third the size of standard Buddleja davidii selections, part of a breeding program aimed at combining full-size flower quality with a dwarf, densely branched frame. Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun, since lean conditions keep growth tight and heavily flowered rather than sprawling. Cut the entire plant back hard to a few inches above ground in late winter, since Buzz series cultivars bloom only on new season's wood and this annual renewal keeps the compact scale intact. Its smaller stature and strong repeat bloom from midsummer to frost make it a reliable choice for patio containers and small mixed borders.

common_name: Buzz Lavender Butterfly Bush (Dwarf Compact Lavender-Purple Buddleja)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Buzz Lavender's condensed size suits small beds and large containers better than full-size davidii selections.

directions: Buzz Lavender opens dense conical spikes of lavender-purple flowers with a warm orange eye against gray-green foliage, on a fountain-shaped shrub bred to roughly a third the size of older Buddleja davidii cultivars while retaining full-size flower quality. Grow in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun, where lean conditions keep the framework tight and densely flowered. Prune the whole plant back hard in late winter, since flowers form only on the current season's growth and this cutback is what maintains the Buzz series' compact scale. Regular deadheading through summer extends bloom and keeps flower color coming steadily until frost.

common_name: Buzz Midnight Butterfly Bush (Dwarf Compact Dark Purple Buddleja)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Buzz Midnight's compact scale fits smaller beds and large containers better than standard butterfly bush.

directions: Buzz Midnight is among the darkest-flowered members of the Buzz series, carrying dense spikes of deep purple blooms with a small orange eye on a compact, densely branched frame roughly a third the size of standard Buddleja davidii selections. Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun, since rich soil or excess shade produces loose, floppy growth at the expense of flower density. Cut the entire framework back hard to a few inches above the ground in late winter, since blooms form only on new season's wood and this renewal keeps the compact habit that distinguishes the Buzz series from full-size butterfly bush. Its dark, saturated color and small footprint make it a strong accent for mixed containers and tight border spots.

common_name: Buzz Purple Butterfly Bush (Dwarf Compact Purple Buddleja)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Buzz Purple stays compact enough for patio pots and small borders without the sprawl of full-size davidii selections.

directions: Buzz Purple bears dense, conical panicles of rich violet-purple flowers on a fountain-shaped shrub bred to a fraction of the size of older Buddleja davidii cultivars while keeping full-size flower quality. Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun, where lean conditions keep the habit tight and heavily flowered rather than lax. Prune the entire framework back hard in late winter, since flowers form only on the current season's growth and this annual cutback is what keeps the compact scale that distinguishes the Buzz series from standard butterfly bush. Deadheading spent spikes through summer extends the bloom season and keeps color coming steadily until frost.

common_name: Empire Blue Butterfly Bush (Classic Violet-Blue Buddleja)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Empire Blue is a vigorous, upright standard-size selection that benefits from an annual hard cutback to control its spread.

directions: Raised in 1941 and still one of the most widely planted blue-flowered butterfly bush cultivars on both sides of the Atlantic, Empire Blue carries dense, honey-scented spikes of violet-blue flowers with a small orange eye on an upright, vigorous shrub with slim, silver-green foliage. Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; rich, moist soil produces rank, floppy growth at the expense of flower density. In colder zones the plant dies back to the base over winter, so cut the entire framework to 12-18 inches in late winter to renew flowering wood and keep the habit upright rather than sprawling. Deadhead through the season to prolong bloom, since spent spikes left in place slow the production of new flowering shoots.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Dartmoor is a large, vigorous selection that needs ample room and an annual hard cutback to stay in bounds.

directions: Dartmoor is instantly distinguishable from typical Buddleja davidii cultivars by its inflorescences: rather than a single terminal spike, each flower head branches into a compound, candelabra-like panicle of magenta to light purple blooms up to a foot long, so heavy that mature branches arch gracefully under their own weight. It grows into a large, vigorous, arching shrub with lance-shaped leaves that are silvery-white beneath, and it earned the RHS Award of Garden Merit for its reliable, showy display. Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun, and cut the entire framework back hard to about 18 inches in late winter, since Dartmoor blooms only on new wood and the yearly renewal is what keeps the branched flower panicles from growing top-heavy. Its butterfly and bee appeal is exceptional even by butterfly bush standards, thanks to the sheer volume of bloom each branched panicle produces.
